newsitem.title: CONGO: France flies out foreigners from Congo-Brazzaville.
newsitem.headline: France flies out foreigners from Congo-Brazzaville.

text.p: France flew out more than 350 foreigners on Monday from the Congolese capital Brazzaville, where gunfire lessened at midday after a morning of shelling.
Bodies of dead fighters and civilians killed in crossfire lay untouched on the streets where they had been shot.
Shooting in the centre of the city lessened although the occasional burst of automatic weapons fire could be heard.
French troops evacuated foreigners to their military base and four French military Transall planes left the city carrying about 90 people in each.

Diplomats said around 300 more French and other foreign nationals were waiting to be evacuated at two hotels in Brazzaville, where fighting has raged for five days between soldiers loyal to President Pascal Lissouba and ex-president Denis Sassou Nguesso's political militia.
They said three companies of French troops had set off for Brazzaville from their base in Bangui, capital of the neighbouring Central African Republic.
"There are about 450 troops on the way to join the 300 who are already here," one diplomat said.
In the Bacongo district, the fiefdom of a militia which has so far been neutral in the fighting, witnesses said a shell had landed killing one person.
One shell landed across the Congo River in Kinshasa, capital of Laurent Kabila's Democratic Republic of the Congo, exploding near the planning ministry. There were no reports of injuries.
France's decision to send more troops to its former colony followed the death of a French soldier in a firefight and reports from French nationals who fled the city of hostility towards them there.
The United States on Sunday ordered non-essential U.S. embassy employees and dependents of embassy personnel to leave and advised other Americans to do the same.
South African oil and chemicals company Sasol Ltd said it had evacuated its four staff because of the violence.

Refugees crossing the river to Kinshasa on Sunday said the fighting appeared to be more widespread than in 1993, when 2,000 people were killed in the capital following disputed parliamentary elections.
There was no clear idea of numbers of dead or wounded.
Clashes began on Thursday after soldiers enforcing a ban on private militias surrounded Sassou Nguesso's house.
Lissouba's government accused Sassou Nguesso in a statement on Sunday of trying to stage a coup and urged the population to rally round the security forces.
"The government informs national and international opinion that it's a question of a coup attempt by Denis Sassou Nguesso who once again wants to take power by force of arms," it said.
"The government asks the Congolese people to stay vigilant and support the security forces to save our young democracy."
A spokesman for Sassou Nguesso said that they were simply defending themselves and demanded that Lissouba admit to being the aggressor as a condition for peace talks.

Sassou Nguesso, a former Marxist military leader, was named president in 1979 but voted out of office in 1992 after the advent of democratic reform. He has accused Lissouba of fomenting violence to postpone the July election.
A national mediation committee was set up on Sunday headed by Brazzaville mayor Bernard Kolelas, runner-up to Lissouba in the 1992 presidential election.
